To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) mobile applications exhibit low TLP and diminishing returns on increasing the number of active cores, 2) big-little core architecture is a promising direction for mobile processors, and 3) the TLP of a mobile application is a good predictor of how many cores it will utilize, which can help in making architectural decisions.
the number of cores used by mobile applications is low and does not increase with increasing the number, and the TLP of the application is low even in heavy-load scenarios.

(1) Mobile applications are utilizing less cores than the number of available cores on average, (2) The utilization of mobile applications does not increase proportionally with increasing the number cores, and (3) The utilization of a single core is not enough to fully utilize the power of a multi-core processor.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: "How can mobile devices benefit from the increasing number of processor cores?"
how many cores should be used to meet the performance needs of mobile applications, and what is the best way to use them.
the design of mobile device SoCs, and the implications of the findings on SoC design.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
current mobile applications do not utilize the available cores to a large extent.
the current mobile workloads are not utilizing the full power and performance of the multi-core mobile SoCs.
the number of cores does not have a direct correlation with the performance gain and power consumption.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
mobile devices have a long way to go before they are able to fully utilize the power of a multicore architecture, and a more flexible architecture would be beneficial.
mobile applications are not yet ready for multi-core processors.
current mobile work loads are not well-suited for multi-core processors, and a new architecture is needed.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, while multi-core mobile devices have become the de facto standard, the performance and energy benefits are not as great as they could be.
the current mobile applications are not utilizing the available parallelism in mobile platforms.
mobile devices should have a limited number of high performance cores and a few low power cores to achieve high TLP, and to save energy during the low TLP phases of an application.
